utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oric, good morning to you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, also good morning to my learned friends from the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I am here together -- included in my team, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink, and our acting case manager, Ms. Sanja Bokulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts, and in the course of the day, our other legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, will join us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So are there any preliminaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would wish to challenge the authenticity of the documents delivered by the Prosecutor on the list of exhibits for examination, and I wish to do so outside the presence of the witness, if I may be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness is not here, so you can proceed. Which documents are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be enumerating all of the documents, and I have the following objection in relation to all the documents. One cannot see the date of drafting of the document, who issued the document, who signed the document, the source is listed as the Serb source; however, the Prosecutor has not shown us the chain of custody in relation to the documents. And the documents are namely 0211 up until 589; then 0211 until 5290. The purported document of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, 8th Operational Group, 282 East Bosnian Brigade. Then document 0211-6740. And the document 0211-6742. There's a list containing 30 names which is unclear. Then the document 0211-6793. Then 0211-6803. Purportedly by the Kazani unit. It's a list of names. Then the following document 0211-6757, and document 0211-6758 which purports to be a list of wounded fighters, members of the armed forces of Srebrenica, dating from 1993. Then document 0211-5743 and document 0211-5746. These are various lists. Then document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me stop you because then it will become too much for me to correct later. The -- in the transcript we are -- when we look at the list ourselves, we are being told, for example, with regard to this last document 0211-5743 and 0211-5764, it shouldn't be 0211-5743, it starts with 02115743. The next thing with regard to this document is, out of the last two digits, 64 or 46? Because on the sheet of paper that we were given by the Prosecution it says "5764." What we heard on the transcript is 5746 and perhaps Mr. Di Fazio can --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can clarify. This is what I said 02115764.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please and if I may be of assistance, these are precisely the documents I intend to start off with this morning, so what I propose, if it's okay, is that I simply go about my cross-examination and I'll produce them into evidence. And then perhaps at the end of the proceedings, Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can refer to the document number -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- As a P-number and if they would put on the record that "We object," it might be simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be more practical if we do it that way because there will be a reference a specific reference to the document number or the exhibit number that way. And I think with regard to the first one I think there was a mistake, too, in the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do it the following way. I will correct this with the court reporter over the break, in order to save time now. And now that I have already started I would like to finish. I have only two more groups of documents remaining, otherwise it will remain unclear for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then document 0211-6784, 02116811 and document 02115908, 02115938, and finally 02115712, 02115712.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So basically I just want to make this clear in my mind. You're not challenging 02115774 to 5781?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we've done that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, you haven't done that. That hasn't been challenged as yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is OTP's P570. I believe that's the document that we announced that we would challenge its authenticity, and we do so now for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So eventually, registrar, please will take note of the corresponding exhibit number that we will give to these documents and my staff will ensure that they are registered as challenged documents. Any further preliminary? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, there is one housekeeping matter for the next witness and it's simply to work out now whether he's likely to testify today and it's because it's not just a question of him but he has two US government representatives who would also attend court and they're waiting to see whether he would be needed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thank you for that observation. In fact I was coming to that myself, waiting to see whether you had anything to say in regard to Lieutenant Colonel Dudley. Mr. Di Fazio, how long are you going to take in having this witness testify? MR. DI FAZIO: Goodly part of the day, but there's a possibility that we might end up if the re-examination is not too lengthy and there's not much from the Bench, then it's possible we might have some time at the end of the day, albeit a shorter period of time, I was thinking maybe half an hour or so, I can't predict with huge certainty. I'm certainly going to go a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you are both aware that we -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- Will finish at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- there will be only one break and we'll finish at 12.15 because I have another sitting afterwards. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that. To make up for the lost time today I am proposing to you that we -- on Wednesday we start at 8.00 instead of 9.00. I hope that is acceptable to both of you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it is necessary, things being what they are. All right? Okay. So when you say that you are aware that we will be finishing at 12.15 today. MR. DI FAZIO: What time do you have the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to have one break in an hour and a half's time from when we started, so about 10.30. MR. DI FAZIO: 10.30 for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Why don't we revisit the situation then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances we could do that easily, with relative ease, I would say, but now we also have the representatives of the American embassy, US embassy, who need to be present, so they need to be advised in a timely fashion. MR. DI FAZIO: Right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wouldn't be very courteous on my part to tell them 15 minutes before come running. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly, Your Honour. I -- in that case, I would say that there is a substantial possibility that we'll find ourselves at the end of today with about half an hour or thereabouts to go with no witness to occupy, unless they're here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that case, may I propose releasing the witness for today, the next witness, and simply we start first thing tomorrow. Because in addition -- I mean, in addition to the matter that it's the two -- in fact three lawyers, US government lawyers and the witness who will be waiting, there's also a question of making arrangements for them to sit in the court and I think it would be more practical just to release everyone for today and we start first thing tomorrow, if Your Honour agrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a more practical approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Of course, from our point of view, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you both. Usher, could you please escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just flag that up for tomorrow that -- for the US government representatives? They were asking where they would be seated in the court and what arrangements would be made to bring them from the lobby, et cetera, and if that could just be taken in hand by the registry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think usually we have them sit where they can -- we can catch their eye with relative ease, if they need to intervene. They could sit over there, over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: They wanted to be somewhere neutral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but somewhere neutral, where would you put them? The only other place is where members of my staff usually sit. That is another possibility, and I think that perhaps is the best solution. And any other member of my staff would sit elsewhere, anyway. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that agreeable to both of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is they do not have eye-to-eye contact with the witness or be able to suggest anything to him. That's all. Yes. Mr. Smajlovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good rest for the weekend. We are going to continue and hopefully finish with your testimony today. May I remind you that you will -- are still testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made the first day you testified, namely to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but truth. Mr. Di Fazio will be proceeding with his cross-examination, and then if it's the case there will be a re-examination and some questions from the Bench. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smajlovic. I was asking you on Friday about some -- about some --

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I was asking you on Friday about some of your colleagues, fighting colleagues. And I want to ask you now about some names and whether you know the people. Sal -- and I may not pronounce the names correctly. I apologise if that causes inconvenience. Do you know a fellow named Salih Zejnilagic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Ibro Salkic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mehmedalija Ulic or Julic?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown this particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would feel, Mr. Di Fazio -- I'm sorry to say it at this late hour in the case, but I've been thinking about this. Sometimes I get the suspicion that you mispronounce - when I say "you" it's not just you, it's several - mispronounce these local names and sometimes this may have been taken advantage of by witnesses. I would prefer if you have these names properly spelled out on a piece of paper -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- that you pronounce it whichever way you like but the witness is shown the name and the surname in -- as it should be. It would make me feel more comfortable that they know exactly who they are being asked about. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that, Your Honour. I think sometimes I'm okay. My colleagues may not -- yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this is Monday morning, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Well, perhaps I'll just show the document to the witness and perhaps with the writing it might be easier. Just if the witness can be shown this one document, just the one document 02116758 and its English translation which is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And many a time I am sure the witness don't -- witnesses don't understand exactly who you are referring to. And I want to put this matter -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, I agree with Your Honour. It's a question of fairness to the witness, too. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There's some handwritten names there. This is a document on -- we don't need to beat about the bush. It speaks for itself. It says "wounded fighters that were members of the Srebrenica armed forces, February 1993," and you can see -- you can see some names there, which I think now might be clear -- clearer. Avdo Smajlovic, that's your father, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find Avdo Smajlovic here anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see it either, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: May I just see what is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is Emir Smajlovic, there is Suad Smajlovic. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand what the problem is. There are two B/C/S documents there. I want to show the witness one. The B/C/S document has the ERN number 02116758, and it consists of four names. And I would ask that Madam Usher put that on the ELMO, and that's the document that I want the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The second page. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- you have the right document now I think and you can see there are four names and it seems to be a list of wounded fighters for February of 1993. Now, you've given evidence about who Avdo Smajlovic is. What about the remainder, the other three names there? Do you recognise any of those names?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do. I don't recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And the document suggests that your father was wounded on the 2nd of February, 1993, at a place called Andrici. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have any knowledge of that. The reason being -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Oh, yes, please. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that my father's wound was quite small. He was simply hit by a stone that must have been set in motion by a shell. And this wasn't even noted that he was wounded. This happened in April when fiercest battles for the defence of Srebrenica took place, when we were all on the defence lines defending the town trying to prevent the Serbs from entering the town. That was the second reason for that. Thirdly, I was not that much concerned with either the lives of my mother or my father but simply to save the people as a whole. I was unable to be with my father at the same spot where he was at the time when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you are tendering this document as one document, I take it? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's how I propose to -- this is a different list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. What's the next number, let me now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P612, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P612. So this document which consists of two pages, one with ERN 02116757 and the other one 02116758, is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P612. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. I'd like to -- perhaps just one other question not in relation to any particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever keep anyone -- or rather, did anyone in your group ever have the job of writing records or keeping records, records relating to membership of your group, the Kazani group?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said so earlier. There were no records kept, no reports written, because we did not have the time for that. We were fighting for our own skin at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you said also that paper was so rare, so rare, that you couldn't even roll cigarettes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said the other time. That's true. We didn't have paper for rolling cigarettes, let alone for writing something on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And that shortage of paper continued throughout 1993 and into -- sorry, throughout 1992 and into early 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only until that date but until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And you certainly would not have had enough paper, if what you say is correct, to create lists such as the one that I just showed you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, we did not have either the time or the paper to do as much, because we were saving our own skins from the attacks on the town of Srebrenica and the general area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. And this paper shortage, such that documents couldn't be created, did that -- was that also in Srebrenica town itself, that's the actual town, not the municipality, but in the town, was it the case that there wasn't -- just simply wasn't paper to write on?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, it was not only in the town of Srebrenica that there was a war, but rather in the general area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: We can get through this quickly. I understand what you're saying, and I understand exactly what you're saying about the harsh conditions and the war, but it's a simple question. This acute shortage of paper was existing throughout 1992, early 1993, and existed in the town of Srebrenica itself. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I had my own group and I was with my group. I wasn't concerned with seeing whether there was paper or not. I was on the front lines trying to save peoples' lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll move on. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, before you move on because there's something about this document that I would like to query. Last line on the first page of this document there is a signature, and there is what looks like the same signature on the other page, too. Perhaps the witness can have a look at that signature or those signatures and tell us whether he recognises that signature. MR. DI FAZIO: I need to follow exactly what Your Honour's saying. Is Your Honour talking about what is now P612, consisting of one page right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes -- consisting of two pages. MR. DI FAZIO: May I see the exhibit, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What we have enrolled, registered as P612 contains two pages, the first one where the witness's name appear, and the second one where his father's name appear. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of -- not exactly at the bottom of that but at the end of the area which is handwritten there is a signature on both pages. If he could recognise -- if he recognises that signature. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's number one. And secondly, I would like you to agree that the English translation of the first page which says at the very end "finished with number 151 (15)" it's -- it is wrong. It shouldn't be 151 but 15, and then it's a bracket, petnaste [phoen] 15 and there is no 15 written on the original. 15 and then open bracket. Do you follow me or not? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it finishes with number 15. Your Honour is looking at March, the March list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. I had in fact intended and I was proceeding on the basis that February and March were going to be different exhibits and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we want, we can change it, but I would suggest that, to avoid confusion, we leave it as it is now. MR. DI FAZIO: It's quicker and I want to move through this as fast as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But does the witness recognise that signature? Have you seen this signature in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I've never seen this signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's it. Let's continue. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd just like to move on to another document now if I may. I'd like the witness to be shown a document bearing ERN number 02116793 through to 02116803, which is a list consisting of 238 names. The translation, if Your Honours please, is incomplete, but it at least has the name of the columns and so on, so you'll be able to work out anything on the remaining pages using that as a guide and we'll undertake to provide you with the full translation as soon as it can be done. Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This document is another list and it seems to be -- claims to be, claims to be, a list of the unit Kazani. Do you see the heading at the top?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And we've -- I don't need to ask you about the obvious things there, but it says that you are the -- I think it says that you are the commander. Is that correct? It says "KDIR."

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was no commander. I was group leader, and it was a group of some 30-odd people. It was no unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, just some of the names, I don't need to deal with all of them, but I just want to ask you about some of them. Do you know a fellow called Hasan Ikanovic, number 3 there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You never heard of such a person?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And Derva Salkic, have you ever heard of such a person?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Go to number 18, Jasmin Bajric, do you see that name, still on the first page. Jasmin Bajric, do you know such a person from Kazani?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What about number 20, Hazim Ahmetovic, was there such a person from Kazani? Is that a real person?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hazim Ahmetovic from Kazani, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just turn over the page, run your finger until you get to 37. You'll see that name again Salih Zjenilagic. Again, that's a name you don't know I think.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know the name. I said so a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, you did, you did. All right. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document which in the B/C/S version starts with 02116793 -- are they all in sequence? Yes, Mr. Smajlovic, would you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I would like to add something. These documents, as they are -- well, in order for a document -- to be a document there always had to be a heading, a signature, and a stamp of the person who drafted the document; that's number two. Number two, such documents could carry a designation "strictly confidential," because these lists contain first and last names. That's as much as I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that information, Mr. Smajlovic. So this document which consists of a handwritten list starting with ERN 02116793 up to and inclusive of 02116805 with a translation into English of part of it consisting of two pages is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P613. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just in that answer that you gave to His Honour you said that documents always required a heading, a signature, and a stamp of the person who drafted the document. Is that -- was that the normal practice in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the customary practice in all professional armies. Since we were local groups, we did not have any HQs, nothing of the sort, and therefore we could not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now -- to show you one other document of a similar nature. MR. DI FAZIO: This, if Your Honours please bears ERN 02116740 through to 6742 and its English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. You can see what the document's about at a glance, I think, Mr. Smajlovic. First of all, let's look at your details. What's the date -- your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4 January -- the 4th of January, 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So whoever wrote this particular document got that particular detail correct. Can you see that in the first column -- second column?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, but I also see it says I was a member of some kind of independent Srebrenica battalion. This is the first time I've heard of such a thing. As far as I know, I was only the leader of a group and it should have said "Kazani" if this document were logical and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. I understand. Thank you for that. And further over it has a column that deals with wounds and it says that you were wounded on two occasions, one in -- the first occasion on the 16th of December, 1992. Now, that detail's correct, isn't it? That's the one -- the wound at Kunjerac?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. And the second -- and it also asserts that on the 24th of March of the following year, 1993, you were wounded at a place called Caus. Now, is that detail correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was wounded only once, in the head.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and I apologise to you. But this calls also for -- okay, no -- I'll stop here. I'll stop here because you haven't made use of it as yet. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about some of the other names that you can see there. Number 13 you've told us you don't know any such person.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Just on the first page, number 9, do you know a fellow called Fikret Kaljevic from Kutlici. Is there any such person?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a place -- you could clear this up for us. Is there a place where there was action at some point in time called Pous, P-o-u-s with a dash on top. I don't know how to pronounce it. MR. DI FAZIO: Where is Your Honours looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am looking at 02116757, which is P612. Number 6, Mr. Di Fazio and Madam Vidovic. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because when you referred the witness to this document that he has in front of him now, you said "Caus." MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to be honest with you, I admire your eyesight because looking at that document I'm unable to decipher what that word is. It could be "Caus," yes, that's true; it could be something else, I don't know. But whatever it is, I think either one or the other requires an explanation. MR. DI FAZIO: Sure, I understand, Your Honours. There is a place called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have never heard of the name "Pous" myself. So I'm asking the question because I want this cleared up. Pous -- MR. DI FAZIO: First of all, there is a place called Caus that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a mountain and we saw it when we were in Potocari. It was pointed out to us. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is there another place that has a similar spelling -- similar spelling or similar word except spelled Pous, P-o-u-s with a dash? Are you aware of any second place called Pous, P-o-u-s with a dash?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you? MR. DI FAZIO: I was dealing, if Your Honours please, with the last one that I wanted to show the witness which was 6757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet, we haven't given it a number yet. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, could that be tendered and be given a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which starts with ERN 02116740 and finishes with 02116742, that's three pages, accompanied by translation thereof into English, another three pages, is being tendered and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P614. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just want to turn now to another issue, and that's the issue of Mr. Akif Ustic. As you know, you've testified last week, that Mr. Ustic was appointed the deputy coordinator at the meeting at Bajramovici, Mr. Oric coordinator, and Mr. Ustic deputy. Do we understand you correctly that he was appointed deputy in charge of coordination amongst the local leaders as well? That was essentially his job, purely and simply, a deputy to Mr. Oric, as Mr. Oric was carrying out his duties as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Akif Ustic was appointed only deputy. That's all that was said at the meeting, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: There was no delineation of what his job was to be? No clear spelling out of his tasks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already answered that question before, Mr. Di Fazio; correct me if I'm wrong, but I think we has already been very clear about it. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He -- Mr. Ustic and Mr. Oric, their working relationship I think you said was not very good because Mr. Ustic did not accept Mr. Oric as his commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just that he didn't accept Oric; he was unable to agree with anyone. He did what he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: He was, therefore, singularly bad at any task involving coordination amongst local leaders? If he didn't get on with anyone, he was probably one of the worst type of people to appoint to that position. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. He was an honourable and honest man. The fact that inter-personal relations were not going well, well, I don't agree with everyone in my company but we still cooperate and everything works.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yeah, but my point is simply this: If Mr. Ustic was to act as a coordinator, deputy coordinator - deputy coordinator - amongst the local leaders, his inability to -- or the fact that he has disagreements with people meant that he wasn't -- a suitable choice. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just repeated again. First of all, I don't agree. If he wasn't on good terms with me for Zulfo or some other leader, maybe there were other leaders whom we don't know about with whom he was on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric ever make any attempt to obtain the services of a deputy whom he did get along with?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that because we were at the lines. We didn't give it much thought. Let me repeat. At that meeting we were supposed to help each other, and this body was supposed to coordinate among the leaders. As I said, if one group had a clash with the Serbs and another village was at risk, we would have to agree on everything. We didn't think about replacing people if they were no good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You just described -- in talking about this you just described this body being supposed to coordinate amongst the other leaders. When you say "this body," are you talking about Mr. Oric and his deputy command -- deputy coordinator, Mr. Akif Ustic, or are you talking about a larger collection of men, this body that you just referred to?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me go back again to what I have just said. The body existed. It was a body headed by Naser Oric, and his deputy was Akif Ustic. This body could do something only if there was a vote. I never said there were more people or lots of people in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. That's clarified. So the body consisted of two people: Mr. Oric and his deputy. Now do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you misunderstood me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's clarify. You were there, you know it best. Tell me: Who was in the body? What was the body made up of? Just tell me the names. Mr. Oric, Mr. Ustic, anyone else? Tell us if there was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no one else in that body, but that body was elected by a large crowd of people, the people in the neighbourhood and the local leaders who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Got you. Thank you very much. You spoke from time to time in your evidence in chief of methods of communication in 1992 and 1993. Do you agree that communications, a system of communications, was essential for the local groups to be able to act together, to fight the Serbs? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no communications at all. We communicated through messages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. I understand what you've said about the state of -- the state of communications. I'm asking you: What would have been desirable, what would have been good to have? Do you agree that having a system of communications would have helped you, would have facilitated, the action of the local groups fighting the Serbs? Thinking back now, do you think that would have been a good thing?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to comment on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why not? It's not difficult. I mean, it's a very simple proposition. All I'm saying to you is this: A system of communication, whatever it be, couriers, radios, or any other method at all, is desirable when local groups, local fighting groups, are working together to fight the Serbs. Would you agree with that basic proposition?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you again, I wouldn't want to comment on that because as I already said we communicated by sending messages and there were no communications among the local groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, I won't press the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I just have a question because it may be a problem of translation. You agreed -- Witness, you agreed that there has been -- may have been messages between different groups. Now -- but you deny today that there was communication. But my question is: Isn't exchanging messages also a form of communication, or do you mean with "communication" something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know and as far as I learned in the professional army from 1997 onwards, communications are considered only means of communication being used to communicate between two persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Yeah, what means of communication are you thinking of? Could you give an example for a sort of communication you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to means of communication used by professional military services. Issuing orders, information, and so on, through means of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I still have a problem. You see, if I send a message to another person and I get an answer from another person, you could call this communication; you communicate between two different people. Now, my question is: When you talk of "communication" and when you say that sending messages back and forth would not be a communication, what do you mean with "communication"? Do you mean the communication needs some technical device or what else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course you need technical devices for communications. These were simply messages. If you tell me to go, I go, but there's no reply. But if you put a question to me through a communication technical device, then I can send you a reply, and then that's communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Judge Eser. Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, I want to wrap this up. Would you agree with me that if you'd have had radios, that would have helped, radio sets using wireless radios, mechanical devices called radios, amongst the local groups, that would have helped you greatly in being able to act together in order to take on the Serbs, to fight the Serbs. Would you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a point where I disagree with you. The configuration of the terrain in Srebrenica is such that in peacetime, before the war, communications did not work properly. In Srebrenica we had a receiver with only one channel and we could never get any other programme, apart from that one channel, because it's in a valley. The Srebrenica area is surrounded by high mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you saying -- are you saying that radio equipment, radio communications equipment, was of little use in the Srebrenica area, the Srebrenica area, and areas where you saw action because of the geography, because of the mountains? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. First of all, we didn't have any means of communication. And your question was: Would it have been easier? I explained to you why, even if we had had means of communication, how it would have functioned. But, I repeat, we had no communication devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Yes. I understand that. Thank you. So did you try and overcome that by using a system of couriers? And I'm talking about the local fighting groups of course. Did they try to overcome the lack of communications with each other by introducing a system of couriers?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. There were no couriers. A courier is also a means of communication. We communicated through messages. If a village was attacked, somebody came and said the village was attacked. There was no return information. Nobody responded saying whether they would come to help or not. These were just ordinary people coming to ask for help when they were under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the PTT building in Srebrenica town?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, no; before the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever see any radio communications systems in that building?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Before the war I only went to the post office to pay my bills, my utilities. I never saw any means of communication there or anything like that. It was never in the public part of the building. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The local fighting groups held -- contained a number of policemen, didn't they? You were one of -- you were a policeman and other policemen also fought in other local groups, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you mean policemen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Policemen, policemen. Policemen who wear uniforms and guns and who go around patrolling the streets and maintaining order. Policemen, such as yourself, were in the local fighting unit, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the role of a policeman only before the war. I had no role as a policeman at that time nor was I a policeman at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, he may have misunderstood you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question was not clear with respect to policemen. It was not clear whether it referred to people who had been policemen before the war or during the war, and the witness understood it the same way I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I agree with you. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- 100 per cent, Ms. Vidovic. Perhaps you may wish to rephrase -- MR. DI FAZIO: It was clear in my mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't -- and I waited for the witness to answer to confirm to myself that he had completely misunderstood you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, and I accept that and I can see how he did. But I think now the matter has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, did those former policemen during the war in 1992 make use of any police radio equipment from their days as policemen earlier, from their time as policemen I should say?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the last part of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did any of the policemen who used to work in Srebrenica before the war started and who fought in local units take with them to the local units police radio sets?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. We had no means of communication and we were not the last persons to be in the police. I reported to work on the 16th, and then I left and all the equipment remained there. After that, as far as I know, the Serbs -- or rather, the Chetniks entered the town and looted everything that could be looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. Let's move on. We've got a lot of ground to cover, which we need to. The -- you testified about the bicycle-driven radio system that you had, and that was -- using that you could hear battlefield reports. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness spoke about a transistor, not a radio system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, agreed. MR. DI FAZIO: Agreed. I won't call it a radio system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But this transistor is the same sort of thing as a radio. You put it on your head, and you listen to waves coming through the air, and you can hear language. Correct? You can hear what Serbs are saying?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, tell us what it is. Tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know, when you put a headset on, that's a Walkman and you can play a cassette or a CD on it. I have never seen anyone listening to the radio like that, at least at that time, before the war or during the war. I saw a Walkman with earphones only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Forget transistors or Walkmans. This device that was operated through a bicycle providing it energy, did it pick up Serb radio communications, whatever the device was?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you it was a transistor and you could listen to the news, yes. But it was not the frequency on which the radio communications operated in the way I learned in the army. These were media frequencies, and something like that could not operate on that frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So -- that's what I was trying to get at. You see, you weren't actually listening in to Serb military radio communications with this bicycle-driven device; you were just listening to Serb mass media that -- the public radio that was being broadcast. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we could listen to their news. That was the area under their control and they had this frequency used by the mass media, which broadcast their public news that we could listen to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And it was from that that you got the information that you can tell us, that you've told us in court about concerning the composition and formation of Serb units. Do I -- is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the information, I stated here, we learned from hearing the news about certain units being set up in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the Serbs were obviously quite happy to publicly broadcast information about their -- the composition of their fighting forces? They didn't shrink from making that public, obviously, at the time?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. Even today, as well as before and during the war, regular armies broadcast their own shows in which they illustrate the size and strength of their units. Likewise, the Serbs had their broadcasts where they talked about their units, about setting up units, and the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I understand better now. So this was Serb propaganda that was being basically broadcast across the airwaves, public propaganda -- public Serb propaganda concerning the composition of their units, their fighting forces?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you in saying that it was propaganda. The way I saw it, these units existed because I clashed with them, and I don't believe that any state would call illustrating a reality propaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have a clash in the making of -- what the meaning "propaganda" is. Propaganda doesn't necessarily mean, at least in the -- in my mind, the spreading of false information. MR. DI FAZIO: No, I understand that. I don't -- and I don't -- I don't adopt that meaning myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's move I think. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm going to. I'm going to move right on, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If I suggested to you that you and other fighting Muslim forces in the Srebrenica area had the means -- the means of radio communication to, A, communicate with each other; and B, that gave them the capacity to listen in to Serb military traffic, communications traffic, would you agree or disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd agree in so far that we were able to listen to the newscasts over the transistor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. One other issue that I think we can briefly deal with before the break. You were shown a document, Exhibit P73, and you were asked to look at the signature on that document. It's -- obviously you can see from it. I'll remind you. On the face of it it claims to be the signature of Mr. Oric, and you were able to tell us that you would never say that it looked like his signature. You were talking -- you gave that evidence, didn't you, purely and simply on the basis of what the signature looked like? That's all. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that I was familiar with Naser Oric's signature because we had worked together on the police force, and he wrote reports there. I didn't say anything else in connection with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just show it to you again. It won't take a moment. MR. DI FAZIO: Could the witness be shown P73, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have a look at the signature again. Can you see it? If you'd like to actually pick it up and look at it closer, feel free, okay, but at the moment it's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see only a small portion of the signature, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, that was going to be my next question, in fact. It's not a very good example, is it, of any signature? The document's a copy, first of all, and it's only half the signature. Now, bearing that in mind, it not being a very good copy and it being only a portion of the signature, do you think it might be Mr. Oric's signature, bearing those factors in mind?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I wouldn't say this was Naser Oric's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Well, now, why? Why do you say that? Because it's not the way he used to construct his signature? And I -- I understand that you're not a forensic expert, handwriting expert, and neither am I, but -- so you're just saying that on the way it looks, the way it appears. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat. I am familiar with his signature because I used to work with him and write reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Right. Is this a fair comment: Do you say it doesn't look anything like his signature? It's just not the way he ever wrote his signature?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wouldn't claim that this was his signature, but I didn't say that it resembled or less his signature. The point, in fact, is that it is not quite visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that then. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you very much, Madam Usher. And I think we've got time for one more topic before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You -- I want to return to the meeting at Bajramovici [Realtime transcript read in error "Bajra Odemici"] in 1992. Your comments were that some groups were not included in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you gave evidence of a number -- I think you actually told us the names of some of the groups. Was there any attempt to get the groups that had not attended at the meeting to become party to this agreement to have Mr. Oric as coordinator?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the area of Srebrenica was cut off internally and that some villages in the area were cut off from others, since there was Serb villages placed in between. That's number one. Number two, the villages of Srebrenica are some 40, 50, 60, or 30 kilometres away from that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, and I understand what you've said about difficulties of moving through the terrain at that time, the dangers and so on. But notwithstanding those difficulties, did anyone make any attempt to bring these groups into -- to make them part of this agreement. Did they try to get through the territory to the distant groups and include them as part of this collection of groups who were going to be coordinated by Mr. Oric?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was not discussed at the meeting and I don't know anything about it. MR. DI FAZIO: Mr. Wubben has detected a spelling mistake, if Your Honours please, it should be Bajramovici, not Bajra Odemici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he said. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said something, Mr. Smajlovic, what was that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No, don't worry, that was for something else. The -- well, I put it to you that if what you say is true and I don't accept what you say about the meeting and the collection of local groups, that it would have -- and what you have said about Mr. Oric being a coordinator, but even on your own account wouldn't it have been crucial to go out and bring these other groups in, to make them part of this agreement, so that there could be greater coordination with all of the groups in the area? Wouldn't that have been a matter of life and death, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat. Had there not been any Serbs in the area, there would probably not have been any war either. However, given the fact that the whole area was cut off internally, there was not much one could do about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, would this be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: May I proceed, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did Mr. Oric ever own a black Mercedes Benz in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you sure of that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you would be a person who would know that, wouldn't you, because you knew Mr. Oric quite well and you even had details about his car ownership, including the fact that he drove a Renault, brought it to Srebrenica, and that his father owned the Renault dealership. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. His father had a car repair shop. It wasn't a dealership. This is an entirely different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you. I understand. No problem. No worries. Anyway, one thing's for sure: He only drove around in a Renault. Correct? You never saw him in a black Mercedes Benz?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was in a Renault that he came to work and went from work, and while he was working he drove it around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown an excerpt from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could you identify the time you are talking about. MR. DI FAZIO: With the Renault?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: With the Renault. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When did he own the Renault? When did he drive around with that?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he arrived in Srebrenica, at the end of 1991. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If I were to show you a video which depicts Mr. Oric on a horse, and in the background there appears to be a car that seems like a black Mercedes Benz, would that affect -- that wouldn't affect your opinion one way or the other about whether or not Mr. Oric owned a black Mercedes Benz, because you're certain, aren't you, that he didn't?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm certain that he didn't. He could have been posing for photos anywhere, just as today he could be taking a photo of -- with a car or something similar in the background.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Let's turn our attention to Bjelovac. You were - and I'm talking about Bjelovac in December of 1992 - you personally made the decision to take your group to the area of Bjelovac. You didn't discuss that with anyone. There was no planning or order from anyone, and you engaged there in fighting for two days or thereabouts. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Nobody gave me any order for that. It was my own decision, and the men who went along with me did so of their own free will. Nobody forced them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you went there to help the refugees, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just explain to the Trial Chamber, please, what precisely you had in mind for your group by going there and how your group was going to assist the refugees, what it was that you were going to do.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was upon Midhat Salihovic's message, who had a group in the area, that I went over there to lend him a hand and to help the people there who were in large groups. There were large groups of refugees in the surrounding woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I heard all of that, but I want to know is -- what I want you to do is explain to the Trial Chamber what precisely you were going to do in order to help Mr. Salihovic and in order to assist the large groups of refugees. Were you going to fight Serbs? Did you attack Bjelovac? Anything in particular? I want to know the particulars of what you were going to do to assist Mr. Salihovic and the large group of refugees.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing specific in it; it was always very spontaneous. I went over to help him because Bjelovac was a large military stronghold and our aim was to stop them from shelling from over there and killing people, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, Kunjerac, not Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness stated "Kunjerac," instead of Bjelovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, both the interpreters and you, Ms. Vidovic. Let's proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So you would be very surprised to see any documentation concerning any planning that took part that occurred with respect to this operation or action or whatever -- event?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I never attended any meetings. There was nothing in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thanks. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P84.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, this is a handwritten document that I want to show you, and I'd like you to look, please, at the -- MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the page that has a computer number on it 02115088. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, if you're interested -- if you want to know where in P84 it is, it's page 35 of the translation, and it has the ERN number 03090739.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If I can assist Madam Usher, it's 02115088, and it's minutes of the Srebrenica OS staff meeting held on the 8th of December, 1992. And the English is at page 35 of the translation, page 35. I repeat, we're talking about a meeting, apparently, on the face of the document, held on the 8th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'd like you to run your eyes down that -- just read it, and also the following page, which in B/C/S has a computer number 02115089, and then the page after that as well, 5091. MR. DI FAZIO: And if Your Honours please, in the English it's pages 35, 36, and 37 -- I apologise, if Your Honours please, and I apologise to Madam Usher. Let me start again. I'm sorry. I'm going to start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The document I want to show you is P84. The B/C/S version is 5 -- ends in 5091. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours will find it as page 37 and 38 of the English. I apologise for that. It's the 10th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, what this document claims to be -- well, this part of the document claims to contain the minutes of the Srebrenica OS staff meeting held on the 10th of December, 1992. That should be in the B/C/S version, ending in 5091, the ERN. And it talks about the planning of an ambush and military-type activities in Voljavica and Bjelovac. It refers to Osmaca units. It refers to things like Mis destroying a tank. It refers to matters such as attacking Bjelovac from the Drina. It has comments from -- apparently comments from some people, including at the bottom of the page a comment from Zulfo. "The houses should not be set on fire. If we capture them early, we will all have to stay one night and in the morning continue towards Sase. We need good guides. All of Bjelovac should be attacked from the Drina." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it a translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I gathered so much. Could we have your help, Ms. Vidovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this part of the diary is mistranslated, quoting Zulfo it says: "Houses should not be torched." It doesn't say "if we take them." It says "if we take, we must spend the night, and in the morning go frontally to Sase." This is suggesting taking the place, not taking the houses, which is quite different. And we have drawn the Prosecutor's attention to such translations. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Please take into account what has been -- MR. DI FAZIO: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't intend to ask you any questions about that. Can you continue reading over the next page which, in the B/C/S version, should have the computer number ending 5092. And you see there a quote from a chap named Osman. And there's a reference there to Soson's men to go with Hajro. It refers then to an ambush in Voljavica containing details about it. 100 men and two ambushes, Mido and Semso with 20 men. And then something about you or Soson with 15 men. Do you see that entry? All right. Do you see the entry?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I see it says here is "Soson." I can't make out what it says next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll put it to you so we can get over this document quickly. I put it to you that this -- what is being spoken of here at these two pages is planning for a military activity or operation or event in the area of Bjelovac and that you were a party to that planning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, I never attended any meetings. I only went to help Midhat Salihovic, who had a group in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you? MR. DI FAZIO: Madam Usher, I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You mentioned in your evidence ribbons and you said that your group did not wear ribbons because otherwise people you called the torbari would follow you. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that my group did not use ribbons and that some groups may have used them or avoided that because the torbari would put on the same kind of ribbons and then it would be impossible to distinguish a fighter from a torbar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. That's what I'm interested in. Do I take it from your answer that occasionally some of these local fighting units wore ribbons and that that had become a problem because it attracted torbari?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying again, we were not in uniform. We had civilian clothes, and we knew each other without any ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'll make it as plain as I possibly can. Did any of the local groups wear ribbons when they were going into -- when fighting?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. Wherever I went to help, the groups did not have ribbons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. You didn't see that. Did you ever hear of it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I see. So you heard about some of the fighting groups wearing ribbons, and did you hear about the consequences, namely that the torbari would be attracted to them? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know which groups wore ribbons?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know why these groups that you heard about wearing ribbons wore those ribbons? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment on that either because I don't know. I didn't see it. I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. If Serb forces wanted to -- sorry, if Muslim forces wanted to -- if Muslim forces wanted to carry out surprise attacks on Serb positions or Serb forces, it was essential to maintain the element of surprise, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, you remember your evidence of the problem of civilians gathering around fighters and that fact bringing down Serb shells on their heads with all the casualties and wounded that you describe. Do you remember that evidence? If you want I'll read it out for you word for word, but I'm just reminding you of it.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. I know exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, if you were to carry out an operation, a military operation, or -- against Serb forces, it was important, wasn't it, that the Serbs didn't know that you were there before you started the operation, wherever it might be?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, it was all spontaneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, when you went to Kunjerac with this group of civilians following you, did -- were you subjected to shelling?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was yelling at the civilians who had taken refuge somewhere in the woods, but not for a moment did I say that they had followed me there or where they went or where they were at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So on this particular occasion you were able to get to Kunjerac without being detected and bringing Serb shells down upon you. Do I -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the area where Midhat's group was I arrived with a group of my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let's forget about Kunjerac for a moment. Did you ever conduct any other activities, your Kazani group, where you were able -- where you wanted to attack Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me interrupt you. I noticed Ms. Vidovic -- do you -- is there a problem, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't really following what Mr. Di Fazio was asking the witness, so it wasn't clear to me, the previous question, but evidently the witness the didn't understand it either. But it's not important to the Defence. It seems that the interpretation is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but if it's not correct, let's go through it and see where it isn't correct because I want to make sure that if there's a question asked that Mr. Di Fazio is thinks is clear and the witness -- the witness cannot possibly understand, well, I mean, we have to look into the matter. Even if it's not of any --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor can put the question again, it seems to me that it's not clear. It seems that he was asked whether he arrived at Kunjerac without any Serb shelling, that he was not noticed. And the witness replied that he got there on his own, and I don't understand from this whether it attracted shelling or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. Yes, I think Ms. Vidovic is right because if you notice from the transcript -- I don't think he -- the Witness actually answered any of the questions that you put. So let's go to the previous page, page 42, line 17, and we start from there. That -- this first part is clear enough. "Well, when you went to Kunjerac with this group of civilians following you, were you subjected to shelling?" His answer: "I said that I was yelling at the civilians who had taken refuge -- who had taken refuge somewhere in the woods, but not for a moment did I say that they had followed me there or where they went or where they were at that point in time." Again, in itself this is already confusing. And then your question: "So on this particular occasion you were able to get to Kunjerac without being detected and bringing Serb shells down upon you?" And not being. "Is that correct?" And his answer is: "I know in the area where Midhat's group was. I arrived with a group of my men," which is again not answering your question. And then of course "let's forget about Kunjerac for a moment, did you ever conduct any activities," et cetera, and so on and so forth. It seems you are taking two completely different directions. You are asking one thing and he is answering another, and no consequence after that either. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kunjerac with your group of men, were you accompanied by civilians, the group of civilians who you had -- who you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said where I observed the group of civilians going behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I didn't ask you where you observed them. It's a simple question, Mr. Smajlovic, and where -- I need to -- we need to make progress and finish my questions and I'm sure you want me to do that. I'll ask the question again. When you arrived at Kunjerac - Kunjerac - the mountain overlooking Bjelovac, that place, that location, with your fighting men, were you at that point of time, at that geographical location, accompanied by civilians? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I arrived there with my group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. That's clarified the matter. Now, forgetting about Kunjerac, I want to ask you about other military activities that you engaged in throughout 1992. On those occasions, did you ever conduct any military activities where it was important that you -- that you maintain an element of surprise and where you did maintain an element of surprise?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I went with my group only to help on the outskirts of Srebrenica, Zanik , Likari, Djogazi, these were attacks on our villages, not attacks by our groups on their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, let's leave Bjelovac and move on to Kravica. You described in -- that you receive add request for assistance from Ejub Golic and that you tried, I think, to -- if I understand your evidence correctly, that you tried to make it to the Kravica area, but you were too weak from your wound to proceed any further. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Ejub Golic sent me a message asking me to help him, and I set out with my group and arrived in the area of Avdagine Njive. That is a Muslim village adjacent to the village of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And on this occasion, bearing in mind that you had no radio equipment whatsoever, did you have any idea what it was that you were going to do in the area?

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just went to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. I've understood your evidence. You said he asked for assistance and you responded with your men. What I'd like to explain to the Trial Chamber is when you set out with your group of armed Kazani fighters to go into battle, into war to face these Serbs with their technical superiority and all of the weaponry they had, it was obviously a grim, dangerous task that you were facing. What plans did you have? What specific plans and actions did you have in mind as you left wherever you were to take your men to the area to go into battle? Explain that to the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: SUAD SMAJLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said just a little while ago, I went with my group to help people. There was nothing to be done on the ground -- or rather, I was fighting, not thinking about what I was going to do. When the Chetniks were attacking our villages or wherever I went to help, when I arrived in the area I would be there defending a hill, a house, a shelter, to stop them from entering a village inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. So basically is it -- I want to understand you correctly, the Trial Chamber wants to understand you. You were going there to help but you didn't actually know what form this help would take beyond fighting, beyond the fact that you would be going to fight.
